title: Continuing my mission of telling you about cool found-space theatre! ...
transcript: in this intimate theatrical experience performed in a series of real life bookstores the audience actually gets to choose the order in which the story unfolds last year, “Edward” played two sold out runs in New York and one in LA and now it's coming back to New York for 20 performances only when the audience arrives we find 27 objects laid out on a table which we’re free to pick up and examine and when the show begins the audience sits in a circle and we take it turns selecting an object each one triggering a story. the performer and creator of the show tells a series of stories from the life of a fictional protagonist named Edward O'connell, each one associated with one of these objects and over the course of the play these non-linear fragments kind of come together to form a collage of one ordinary person's life there's also a clever little device at the end which I won't spoil but kind of heightens the format of the show even more when I saw it it was being done in real life apartments But like I said now they're performing it in a rotating series of real life bookstores and even though it's the same stories being told it really is different every time like after I saw it the artist kind of hung around casually chat about the experience and he talked about how not only is the order different every time but how that can subtly shift the audience's experience like at our performance it was the first time that this particular object had been selected right at the beginning of the show he was commenting on how different the show felt with that being our intro to the character I will say I often struggle with theatre that uses a lot of narration and I felt that here sometimes, there were some stories where I was having trouble staying engaged but I think the format and the kind of complete picture that we get helped me stay locked in for the journey overall. but if you wanna see your own iteration of Edward it's playing January 21st through February 24th in New York via Ed Schmidt Theatre Company
